Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' implies a trauma context involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty/survivor scenario, which is hard to reconcile with the stated index trauma of sexual assault in the absence of any supporting items about others dying. This is a trauma-type mismatch rather than a merely unusual appraisal.

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' can function as a trigger in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other triggers are perfume/cologne and body pain, while threat is dominated by touch/startle/flashback phenomena and appraisals focus on emotional numbing and self-reliance. The positive-affect trigger is not impossible, but in this item set it lacks a clear clinical link and looks mismatched to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The flashback item is not inherently implausible for sexual assault PTSD, but in this profile the rest of the network is strongly organized around hypervigilance to touch/body danger and negative appraisals, with no memory items and no trigger-to-memory/threat linkage in the formulation. A full reliving-style flashback can coexist, but here it sits somewhat at odds with the otherwise body/startle-centered pattern and appears insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

vignette:
Tariq is a 27-year-old Palestinian-American man who works as a licensed physical therapist at an outpatient rehabilitation clinic in suburban Chicago. He has been married for two years to his wife, Lena, and by most external measures his life before the assault appeared stable and purposeful. He presented for an initial psychological evaluation eight months after a sexual assault that occurred during a work-related social event, describing his current distress as "getting worse, not better" and expressing significant ambivalence about whether treatment could help someone like him.

The assault took place at a colleague's apartment following a small gathering after a professional conference. Tariq had accepted a drink from a coworker he trusted, and at some point in the evening he lost full continuity of awareness. He regained consciousness in a back bedroom, in pain, with another man present. The physical pain was acute and localized. A heavy, sweet cologne - the kind worn by the man in that room - was thick in the air. He did not fully understand what had happened to him for several hours afterward, and when comprehension settled in, it arrived not as a single realization but as a slow, nauseating accumulation of evidence. He told no one for six weeks.

In the months that followed, the assault did not recede so much as it redistributed itself across the ordinary surfaces of his life. At the clinic, Tariq works closely with patients' bodies - repositioning limbs, applying manual pressure, guiding movement through resistance. Several times a week, a patient arrives wearing a cologne that carries the same dense, floral-musk quality as the one from that night, and without warning Tariq finds himself no longer fully in the treatment room. His hands continue their work, but something behind his eyes goes flat and distant. He has learned to finish the session on a kind of autopilot, telling himself afterward that it happened to someone else - a younger version of himself, perhaps, or a man he once knew. This framing offers momentary relief, though the relief never fully holds. On days when a patient's rehabilitation involves hip or pelvic work, and Tariq must apply pressure to areas of the body that mirror his own site of injury, a wave of physical sensation can arrive that is indistinguishable, in the moment, from what he felt that night. He has begun scheduling those particular patients with a colleague when possible, offering vague explanations about caseload management.

At home, intimacy with Lena has become something Tariq approaches with dread and then avoids entirely. He had come to believe that his body was no longer his own in any reliable sense - that it had been made into something that could be used without his knowledge or consent, and that this fact was written into him permanently. The shame he carries is not abstract. It is located specifically in his body, in the parts of himself that were touched, and he finds it almost impossible to tolerate Lena's physical closeness without a creeping sense of contamination that he cannot explain to her and has not tried to. Their marriage, once warm and physically affectionate, has grown quiet and careful. Lena has asked questions he has not answered.

Tariq is hypervigilant in ways that now feel involuntary. In the clinic hallway, if a door swings open suddenly, or if a patient reaches toward him without warning, his body responds before his mind can intervene - a sharp flinch, a step back, a moment of braced readiness that he then has to explain away with a joke. He scans the room when he enters it. He sits with his back to walls.

What finally brought him to seek help was a session three weeks ago in which a patient unexpectedly touched his forearm to steady himself, and Tariq, without meaning to, said "don't." The patient looked confused. Tariq completed the session and then sat in his car for forty minutes. He was certain, in that parking lot, that he was no longer capable of feeling the way he once had - that warmth, ease, and trust had been replaced by something permanent and mechanical. He came to the first session hoping to be told he was wrong about that, and terrified that he would not be.
